1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 25-year-old young man who was previously healthy, with no significant past medical history. He denied a history of TB or close contact exposure, denied a history of trauma, and denied a history of blood transfusion. He had no history of drug allergy. He denied smoking and alcohol use, and denied contact with epidemic areas. He was unmarried and had no family history of hereditary disease. On Day 0, the patient presented to Guangzhou Military Region General Hospital for neck pain with limited mobility for more than 1 month. Whole-body PET/CT showed "multiple osteolytic bone destruction of the occipital bone, cervical vertebrae, and thoracic vertebrae, with associated soft tissue mass formation and mildly increased metabolism." On Day +5, a biopsy of the cervical mass indicated "epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone." For further diagnosis and treatment, the patient presented to the Orthopedics Department of our hospital on Day +25 of the same year. Multiple tumors of the occipital bone and cervical vertebrae (occipital bone, C1-7) were considered. Because the examination suggested abundant blood supply to the lesions and high surgical risk, radiotherapy was recommended first. Therefore, the patient came to Navy 411 Hospital on Day +28 for radiotherapy for the cervical tumor. However, unexpectedly for the patient and his family, after only 1 session of radiotherapy, the patient developed sudden chest tightness and shortness of breath, worse after activity, with occasional dry cough, without fever or night sweats, without hemoptysis or chest pain, and without bilateral lower extremity edema. Pleural ultrasound showed "a large right pleural effusion." On Day +33, a right chest tube was placed, draining a large amount of bloody pleural fluid. Pleural fluid cytology showed "small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells." Repeat pleural ultrasound 5 days later still indicated bilateral pleural effusions. On Day +38, the patient presented to the Pulmonology outpatient clinic of our hospital for further diagnosis and treatment, with the chief complaint of "cervical tumor discovered for more than 1 month, chest tightness and shortness of breath for more than 10 days." He was admitted with the outpatient diagnosis of "pleural effusion, etiology to be determined." Since onset, the patient had poor energy, no significant change in body weight, normal appetite, normal bowel and bladder function, and no obvious sleep disturbance. I. Findings on admission examination: Temperature 36.7℃, heart rate 80 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, SpO2 98% (oxygen 4 L/min). He was conscious, in poor general condition, and was transported into the ward on a gurney. There was no jaundice of the skin or mucosa, no petechiae or ecchymoses, and no palpable superficial lymphadenopathy. Cervical spine range of motion was limited, with positive tenderness and percussion tenderness, and the neck was immobilized with a cervical collar. The trachea was midline, with no jugular venous distention. There was no thoracic deformity. Percussion was dull over both lower lungs, and breath sounds were absent in both lower lungs. Cardiac and abdominal examinations were negative. The extremities moved freely, with no clubbing of the fingers or toes, and no edema of either lower extremity. Neurologic examination was negative. Outside hospital laboratory and ancillary examinations: Whole-body PET/CT (Day 0, at Guangzhou Military Region General Hospital): multiple osteolytic bone destruction involving the occipital bone, posterior arch of the atlas and bilateral transverse processes, multiple transverse processes, vertebral arches, and spinous processes of C2-7, and the right transverse process of the T2 vertebral body, some with pathologic fractures and associated soft tissue mass shadows, with mildly increased metabolism; a primary bone lesion was considered, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis could not be excluded. Cervical spine CT (Day -2, at Zhongshan Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Zhongshan, Guangdong): multiple bone destruction involving the occipital bone, posterior arch of the atlas, spinous processes of C2-6, and bilateral transverse processes of C7; multiple areas of bony discontinuity in the spinous processes of C2-6; adjacent soft tissue swelling; intermediate or malignant tumor considered. Cervical spine tumor pathology (Day +17, at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center): the lesion was consistent with hemangiomatous change. Cervical spine tumor pathology (Day +10, at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University): the lesion was consistent with intermediate hemangioendothelioma. Pleural ultrasound (Day +38, at Navy 411 Hospital) indicated bilateral pleural effusions. Pleural fluid cytology indicated the presence of small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells.

differential_diagnoses.name: Malignant pleural effusion (associated with malignant bone/soft tissue tumor; pleural involvement or metastasis related to a vascular-origin tumor is the primary consideration)
supporting_evidence: Chest ultrasound showed "a large right pleural effusion," and repeat examination 5 days later still indicated "bilateral pleural effusions."
Large-volume bloody pleural effusion drained via right pleural catheter
Pleural fluid cytology showed "small cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells"
PET/CT showed "multiple osteolytic bone destructions in the occipital bone, cervical vertebrae, and thoracic vertebrae, with associated soft tissue mass formation"
Prior pathology of the cervical spine tumor suggested "epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone" and "intermediate hemangioendothelioma".

The patient developed chest tightness and shortness of breath, worsened after activity. On physical examination, percussion dullness was present over both lower lungs, and breath sounds were absent in both lower lungs, consistent with the clinical presentation of massive pleural effusion.
opposing_evidence: Pleural fluid cytology suggested "small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells," which was not completely consistent with the previously reported vascular-origin tumor type on cervical vertebral pathology.

There are discrepancies among the cervical spine pathology results: they were reported at different times as "epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone", "hemangioma-like changes", and "intermediate hemangioendothelioma"

differential_diagnoses.name: Epithelioid hemangioendothelioma/intermediate-grade hemangioendothelioma with multifocal osseous involvement and pleural involvement
supporting_evidence: On Day +5, biopsy of a cervical spine mass indicated "epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone"
On Day +10, pathology of the cervical spine tumor indicated: "The lesion is consistent with epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, intermediate grade."
Imaging showed multiple osteolytic bone destructions in the occipital bone, cervical spine, and thoracic spine, accompanied by soft tissue mass formation, consistent with aggressive osseous lesions.
The lesion was described as having a rich blood supply, suggesting the possibility of a vascular tumor.
On the basis of preexisting multiple bone lesions, bilateral pleural effusions and dyspnea subsequently developed, suggesting possible pleural or pulmonary involvement.
opposing_evidence: Pleural fluid cytology indicating “small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells” is not a typical cytologic description of vascular endothelial tumor.
Another pathology report indicated only "hemangiomatous change," and there is inconsistency between the pathological diagnoses.

differential_diagnoses.name: Primary small cell lung cancer with pleural metastasis/malignant pleural effusion; bone metastasis to be considered
supporting_evidence: Pleural fluid cytology indicated detection of "small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells"
The patient developed chest tightness, shortness of breath, occasional dry cough, and bilateral pleural effusions.
PET/CT showed multiple osseous destructive lesions; bone metastases from malignant tumor should be considered
opposing_evidence: The patient is only 25 years old and has no smoking history, which is not consistent with the typical epidemiologic characteristics of small cell lung cancer.
No imaging evidence of a primary intrapulmonary lesion was provided in the phase 1 data.
Previous pathology of the cervical spine mass indicated a vascular tumor, suggesting that the bone lesion may not have been caused by bone metastasis from lung cancer.

differential_diagnoses.name: Angiosarcoma/malignant vascular neoplasm (multiple osteolytic bone destruction with bloody pleural effusion)
supporting_evidence: Multiple osteolytic bone destruction with associated soft tissue mass formation, suggesting an aggressive malignant tumor
The lesion has an abundant blood supply, supporting the possibility of a vascular tumor.
Thoracic drainage yielded a large amount of bloody pleural effusion; bloody pleural effusion can be seen in invasive vasoformative malignant tumors

Prior pathology findings varied among “hemangioma-like change,” “intermediate hemangioendothelioma,” and “epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone,” suggesting the need for differential diagnosis within the spectrum of vascular tumors.
opposing_evidence: In the first stage, there was no definitive pathology directly supporting "angiosarcoma".
Pleural fluid cytology suggested "small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells," which is not directly consistent with angiosarcoma

differential_diagnoses.name: Tuberculous pleuritis/tuberculosis-related pleural effusion
supporting_evidence: The patient is a young adult with chest tightness, shortness of breath, dry cough, and bilateral pleural effusions; tuberculous pleuritis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pleural effusion.
opposing_evidence: The patient denies a history of TB and close contact exposure.
No fever or night sweats; no significant change in body weight.

The pleural effusion was a large-volume bloody effusion, and pleural fluid cytology identified "small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells," which clearly more strongly supports malignant pleural effusion.
The concurrent presence of multiple osteolytic bone destructions and soft tissue masses cannot be adequately explained by tuberculous pleuritis alone.

stage2_input.text: After admission, the following examinations were completed: 1. Blood tests: Complete blood count: WBC 10.7×10^9/L↑, neutrophils% 84%↑, platelets 298×10^9/L, hemoglobin 157 g/L. CRP: 12.55 (0-10 mg/L)↑. ESR: 58 (0-15 mm/h)↑. Liver function: albumin 36 g/L (35-50 g/L), ALT 75 (21-72 U/L)↑, AST 36 (17-59 U/L), GGT 85 (12-58 U/L)↑. Coagulation: PT 12.2 (9-13 s), aPTT 33.4 (20-40 s), thrombin time 24.1 (14-21 s)↑, fibrinogen 4.99 (2-4.5 g/L)↑, D-dimer 5620 (<550 ug/L)↑. Tumor markers: CA125 77.39 (<35 U/mL)↑; NSE, CYFRA211, CEA, CA199, and SCC antigen were normal. Routine urine and stool tests, electrolytes, renal function, alkaline phosphatase, lactate dehydrogenase, parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, BNP, serum protein electrophoresis (IgA, IgM, IgG, IgE, κ, λ, κ/λ), and M protein showed no obvious abnormalities. Hepatitis B serology, HIV, and HLA-B27 were negative. 2. Imaging: 1) Thoracoscopy (Day +39): left-sided hemorrhagic pleural effusion; approximately 1000 mL was aspirated; no obvious pleural abnormality was seen. Routine pleural fluid examination: red turbid appearance, Rivalta test positive ++, RBC 506000×10^6/L↑, WBC 5900×10^6/L↑, lymphocytes 65%↑, segmented neutrophils 24%, macrophages 11%, atypical nucleated cells seen↑. Pleural fluid biochemistry: albumin 28 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 532 U/L, glucose 6.8 mmol/L. Pleural fluid tumor markers: CA125 2032 U/mL↑, CYFRA211 12.79 ug/L↑; CEA, CA199, and SCC antigen were normal. No cancer cells were seen on three pleural fluid cytology examinations. 2) Cervical spine MRI: large patchy abnormal signal shadows were seen in the appendages from C1 to T1 and the visualized occipital bone and surrounding soft tissues, with poorly defined margins; T1WI showed low signal, T2WI showed heterogeneous high signal; partial appendage defects were present in this region; contrast-enhanced scan showed heterogeneous marked enhancement of the lesions. 3) Chest CT: bilateral pulmonary inflammation with bilateral pleural effusions; localized bilateral pleural thickening. Abdominal ultrasound: no obvious abnormality. 4) Pleural fluid (our hospital, Day +45): On Day +42, the patient reported worsening dyspnea and chest tightness. Repeat pleural ultrasound showed reaccumulation of a large left pleural effusion, and a left pleural drainage tube was placed for drainage. On Day +45, chylous pleural fluid was drained from the left side, and the chyle test was positive.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: On Day +45, whole-body PET-CT showed multiple abnormal signals in the occipital bone, cervical vertebrae, and thoracic vertebrae, considered to be tumor.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 25-year-old young adult who initially had persistent neck pain and limited range of motion for more than 1 month, and then rapidly developed chest tightness, dyspnea, and recurrent massive bilateral pleural effusions after 1 session of radiotherapy for a cervical spine lesion. The disease progressed rapidly, suggesting possible systemic osseous lesions with thoracic involvement. Previous imaging had already indicated multiple osteolytic destructive lesions and soft tissue masses in the occipital bone, cervical spine, and thoracic spine, and pathology was inconsistent among epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone, hemangiomatous change, and intermediate hemangioendothelioma. In addition, pleural fluid cytology at an outside hospital suggested small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells. Clinically, it is first necessary to determine whether the lesions represent multicentric neoplastic disease and whether there are other primary or metastatic lesions. Whole-body PET-CT can provide an overall assessment of the distribution and extent of the lesions, metabolic activity, and whether there is concomitant pleural, pulmonary, or other site involvement, helping to distinguish primary bone disease, metastatic carcinoma, or other systemic diseases, and providing a basis for subsequent biopsy site selection, assessment of surgical/radiotherapy risk, and formulation of a treatment strategy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Cervical spine tumor biopsy indicated "epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone".
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient's cervical spine lesion was the earliest and most clearly defined focal lesion, accompanied by marked neck pain, limited range of motion, tenderness, and multiple sites of osseous destruction on imaging, with some cases also accompanied by pathologic fracture; the lesion was highly vascular, and local surgical risk was high. Because the pleural effusion was initially bloody and later became chylous, the pleural fluid cytology results were contradictory over time, while pathology of the bone lesions had at different times suggested epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone, hemangiomatous change, and intermediate hemangioendothelioma, the central clinical question was whether the bone lesion represented a malignant tumor, a vascular intermediate lesion, or an atypical osteolytic disease. Biopsy of the cervical spine tumor could directly obtain histopathologic evidence to clarify the nature of the lesion, explain the relationship between the osseous destruction and the pleural complications, exclude differential diagnoses such as metastatic carcinoma, and provide decisive evidence for whether surgical reconstruction, radiotherapy, or other targeted treatment would be needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: On Day +45, in the patient’s two previous pleural effusion cytology examinations, no malignant cells were identified. In conjunction with the outside hospital pleural effusion cytology indicating detection of small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells and the pathology slide results, please request a pathology consultation to assist with diagnosis and treatment.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After treatment for a cervical spine lesion, the patient rapidly developed chest tightness and shortness of breath. Pleural ultrasound showed large bilateral pleural effusions. Tube drainage yielded a large amount of bloody pleural fluid, and chylous-appearing pleural fluid subsequently developed, indicating that the pleural effusions were not only large in volume but also complex in character, making this the key issue currently affecting the clinical course and diagnostic direction. Pleural fluid cytology at an outside hospital had suggested small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells, but after admission, three pleural fluid cytology examinations all showed no malignant cells, which was clearly inconsistent with the prior bone pathology and the overall clinical presentation. Therefore, pleural fluid cytology must be reviewed and repeated. The clinical objective of this test is to determine whether the pleural effusion is malignant pleural effusion, to clarify whether the outside hospital result reporting 'carcinoma cells' is reliable, and to assist in differentiating metastatic carcinoma/primary lung cancer, pleural involvement by a vascular-origin tumor, and non-neoplastic chylothorax. The result will directly affect whether further evaluation and treatment should proceed along a malignant tumor pathway and whether more aggressive pleural tissue sampling and antitumor therapy are needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: On Day +45, in the patient’s two previous pleural effusion cytology examinations, no malignant cells were identified. In conjunction with the outside hospital pleural effusion cytology indicating detection of small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells and the pathology slide results, please request a pathology consultation to assist with diagnosis and treatment.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The most prominent diagnostic difficulty in this case is the contradiction among multiple pathology reports: the cervical spine lesion was successively described as epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone, hemangiomatous change, and intermediate hemangioendothelioma, while pleural fluid cytology from an outside hospital favored small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma; however, after admission there was a lack of persistent evidence supporting malignancy, and the pleura showed no obvious abnormality on thoracoscopy. Review of the pathology slides is the key step in resolving the diagnostic discrepancy, allowing pleural fluid cytology, the prior bone biopsy, and subsequent pathology to be reinterpreted within the same framework, with multidisciplinary consultation if necessary to further determine whether misinterpretation exists. This evaluation is intended to clarify the true pathologic lineage of the lesion, exclude misdiagnosis of metastatic carcinoma or small-cell carcinoma, determine whether it is more consistent with osteolytic disease caused by abnormal vascular/lymphatic proliferation, and accordingly affect the patient's management plan regarding surgery, radiotherapy, and thoracic duct-related treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: 2. Cervical immobilization, neck protection, repeat cervical spine X-ray, MRI plain scan + contrast enhancement.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has multiple osteolytic bone destructions in the occiput and C1-7, with neck pain, markedly limited range of motion, local tenderness and percussion tenderness, and cervical collar immobilization, indicating a high risk of impaired cervical spine stability; outside-hospital CT also showed multiple areas of cortical discontinuity and some pathologic fractures. The cervical lesion currently is relevant not only to the diagnosis, but also directly to neurologic and spinal cord safety and the timing of subsequent treatment. Repeat cervical spine X-rays can dynamically observe the extent of bone destruction, vertebral alignment, and changes in stability, assess whether there is further collapse, displacement, or deformity, provide basic information for continued immobilization and protection, whether emergency surgical reconstruction is needed, and selection of surgical levels, and also help monitor the evolution of the local lesion after radiotherapy and during disease progression.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: 2. Cervical immobilization, neck protection, repeat cervical spine X-ray, MRI plain scan + contrast enhancement.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The lesion involving the cervical spine and occipital bone is extensive, with an associated soft tissue mass, pain, and functional impairment, and the lesion is highly vascular, with risk of invasion of the spinal cord, nerve roots, spinal canal, and surrounding soft tissues. Although prior CT and subsequent MRI have already shown extensive abnormal signal and marked enhancement involving the posterior elements from C1 to T1 and the surrounding soft tissues, contrast-enhanced MRI in addition to non-contrast MRI remains a necessary examination in the setting of uncertain pathologic nature, complex local anatomy, and planned further surgery/treatment. This examination is mainly used to more clearly demonstrate bone marrow involvement, the extent of soft tissue involvement, enhancement characteristics, whether there is compression within the spinal canal, and the relationship to surrounding critical structures, thereby helping differentiate neoplastic lesions from vascular/lymphatic proliferative lesions, assess surgical risk and resectability, and guide the subsequent reconstruction and internal fixation plan.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Is it Gorham’s syndrome or Gorham disease? We conducted a multidisciplinary discussion, as follows: Orthopedic Oncology: On Day +45, whole-body PET-CT showed multiple abnormal signals in the occipital bone, cervical vertebrae, and thoracic vertebrae, considered to be tumors. Biopsy of the cervical spine tumor suggested "epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone." Evaluation by the Orthopedics Department at our hospital considered multiple tumors of the occipital bone and cervical spine (occipital bone, C1-7). Associate Professor Yang Zaixing from Orthopedic Oncology provided the following consultation recommendations: 1. Further clarify the nature and etiology of the pleural effusion. 2. Neck immobilization, neck protection, repeat cervical spine X-ray, MRI without contrast + contrast-enhanced. 3. Cervical spine tumor biopsy, and referral to Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center to further clarify the cervical spine pathology report. 4. After the pleural effusion is controlled and stable, contact our department for surgical treatment. Pathology: On Day +45, the patient’s previous 2 pleural fluid cytology examinations did not detect cancer cells. In conjunction with pleural fluid cytology from an outside hospital indicating small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma cells and the pathology slide results, a pathology consultation was requested to assist in diagnosis and treatment. Consultation opinion from Chief Physician Jiang Jisheng of the Pathology Department: Reviewed 2 routine smears from PLA 411 Hospital; agreed that the outside hospital diagnosis tended toward small-cell undifferentiated carcinoma. However, after admission, no evidence of malignant tumor was found, so further repeat pathology review was recommended. Thoracic Surgery: On Day +57, whole-body PET-CT showed multiple abnormal signals in the occipital bone, cervical vertebrae, and thoracic vertebrae, considered to be tumors. Biopsy of the cervical spine tumor suggested "epithelioid hemangioendothelioma of bone." Evaluation by the Orthopedics Department at our hospital considered multiple tumors of the occipital bone and cervical spine (occipital bone, C1-7). Chief Physician Zhong Lei from Thoracic Surgery provided the following consultation recommendations: 1. Left pleural effusion, possible chylothorax, 300-400/day; 2. Conservative treatment, treat the bone tumor; 3. Thoracic Surgery follow-up, and if the chylothorax worsens, consider surgical ligation of the thoracic duct.

images.near_text: Figure 4. Pathology of the cervical spine tumor.

diagnostic_basis: Symptoms: shortness of breath and chest tightness for more than 10 days. Young adult, no family history.

Physical signs: limited cervical spine range of motion; tenderness and percussion tenderness positive; dullness to percussion over both lower lungs; breath sounds absent in both lower lungs; no other significant abnormalities.

Ancillary examinations: ① Ultrasound indicated pleural effusion, initially hemorrhagic pleural effusion, later chylothorax; ② PET-CT showed "multiple osteolytic bone destructions of the occipital bone, cervical vertebrae, and thoracic vertebrae"; ③ Pathology of cervical vertebral tumor biopsy: fibrous tissue hyperplasia, with dilated blood vessels observed, and no cellular atypia.
Under general anesthesia, posterior occipital and cervical spine tumor resection, reconstruction, and internal fixation were performed. Postoperative pathology: diffuse angiomatosis

treatment_plan: Bilateral pleural cavity infusion of arsenic trioxide to control pleural effusion
Symptomatic and supportive treatment, including albumin administration to correct hypoproteinemia
Posterior occipital and cervical spine tumor resection with reconstruction and internal fixation under general anesthesia
treatment_response: Dyspnea and chest tightness markedly improved
After intrapleural infusion of arsenic trioxide, the chylothorax was markedly controlled.
